column3: Its portrayal of deniers absorbed in doubt offers only a remote pre-judgment backdrop to their later surrender.
Mutual questioning among the saved loosely contrasts with the accusatory exchange that follows the focus.
The disciples' professed willing submission is a broad positive contrast to the focus's compelled surrender.
The command separating the criminals on that Day directly frames the defeated group described in the focus.
The immediate context gathers wrongdoers, their companions, and their objects of worship for judgment.
It explicitly depicts wrongdoers casting submission before God when their inventions abandon them.
It identifies persistent transgression in deniers but does not address their helpless submission at judgment.
The immediately preceding order to halt them for questioning explains their inability to act freely.
The peaceful response of God's servants uses a different sense of the shared root than coerced surrender.
Their doubt and blindness about the Hereafter provide a distant cause, not the surrendering scene itself.
The believers' recollection of former fear does not clarify the condemned group's compelled surrender.
Abraham and Ishmael's willing yielding to God provides a pointed contrast to the focus's forced yielding.

The command to enter Hell on that Day gives the punitive outcome of the defeated criminals.

Withholding small kindness does not clarify the judgment scene or compelled surrender.
The promise that the deniers will see offers a remote warning related to the future scene.
Wrongdoers cast submission at death while futilely denying evil, a close forced-surrender parallel.
Passing by ruined towns at night does not illuminate the focus's surrender.

Woe for deniers on that Day supplies a general judgment consequence.

Showing off in worship does not clarify forced surrender or the judgment exchange.

Passing the ruins of former peoples does not clarify the focus's compelled submission.

Questioning when the Day of Recompense will come is a general antecedent to the focus.
The believers' predawn seeking forgiveness does not clarify the condemned group's surrender.

The command to be among submitters is a general voluntary contrast.
Thamud's denial of warnings gives a broad pattern leading to judgment, not the focus's submission.

The etiquette of household meals and greetings does not clarify the focus.
The single cry that brings all to sight is the immediate resurrection prelude to their compelled surrender.
Their cry of woe on the Day of Recompense directly supplies the judgment setting of the focus.
The Day of Decision they once denied immediately precedes the gathering, helplessness, and surrender described here.
The declaration that they will taste painful punishment gives the direct consequence of their final subjugation.
It commands submission before punishment comes and states that none will be helped, a near-verbatim thematic parallel.
Leaders are disowned by their followers when punishment is seen and every bond is severed, directly paralleling failed mutual aid.
The followers wish to disown those they followed after seeing punishment, closely matching the focus's collapsed alliances.
People come to God alone, leaving behind the intercessors they claimed, directly illuminating abandonment and helplessness.
Successive guilty communities enter the Fire, curse one another, and share intensified punishment, closely paralleling the focus passage.
The earlier guilty group denies any advantage over the later and confirms shared punishment in the Fire.
On the Day of gathering, idolaters are separated from their alleged partners, who deny being worshipped, directly matching failed allegiance.
The weak ask arrogant leaders whether they can avert any punishment; the leaders admit they are all alike, closely paralleling 37:25-26.
Associators confront their alleged partners, who reject their association, directly preceding the compelled submission in 16:87.
Those invoked as partners cannot answer when called, demonstrating the same futility of relying on others at judgment.
Calling on what can neither harm nor benefit provides the prior false reliance exposed in the focus scene.
God gathers worshippers and the beings they worship and asks about their misguidance, closely paralleling the focus's judgment assembly.
The alleged objects of worship deny that they could take protectors besides God, directly exposing the failure of false allies.
Misleading leaders acknowledge leading their followers astray and disown them, closely matching the admissions in 37:30-32.
The condemned are told to call their alleged partners, who do not answer, directly illustrating their final abandonment.
Wrongdoers stand before their Lord and exchange blame, a close parallel to the focus passage's post-judgment confrontation.
Arrogant leaders deny preventing the weak from guidance, closely paralleling the denial of coercive authority in 37:30.
The weak blame the leaders' plotting and both groups conceal regret when shackles appear, directly extending the focus's collapsed alliance.
Alleged partners cannot answer their callers and will deny their association on the Day of Resurrection, directly clarifying failed recourse.
People take gods besides God hoping for aid, directly setting up the unanswered question of why they cannot help one another.
Those gods cannot help their worshippers, an explicit and close counterpart to the focus's failed mutual assistance.
The people of the Fire argue with one another, closely paralleling the mutual questioning and blame that immediately follow the focus.
Arrogant leaders acknowledge that all parties are in the Fire under God's judgment, directly paralleling their shared helplessness and punishment.
Intimate friends become enemies on that Day except the God-fearing, supporting the focus's collapse of worldly solidarity.
Those invoked besides God become enemies of their worshippers and deny their worship when people are gathered, directly paralleling abandoned false allies.
Satan disowns the person he induced to disbelieve, a close pattern of a misleader abandoning his follower.
